[6, 9] The plant was discovered in September 2023 in two small, adjacent private ponds on residential properties near Berrien Springs in Berrien County. [3] The discovery was made during routine monitoring for another prohibited invasive plant, parrot feather, which had been identified in the ponds in 2020. [6, 7] Michigan State University Extension assisted EGLE in confirming the identification of the hydrilla. [11] In response, EGLE initiated surveys of connected waterways, including the St. Joseph River, and began herbicide treatments to prevent the plant's spread, with a long-term goal of eradication. [5, 6] <2> The Tennessee Department of Agriculture (TDA) officially confirmed the first detection of the invasive spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) in Davidson County on September 28, 2023, making Tennessee the 16th state to identify the pest since its initial U.S. discovery in Pennsylvania in 2014. [3, 5, 7] The confirmation followed a report from a citizen who spotted the insect. [5] This non-native species, originally from Asia, poses a significant threat to various agricultural and natural resources, showing a preference for grapevines, fruit trees, and the invasive Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima). [3, 6, 10] It also affects other trees like maple, black walnut, and yellow-poplar. [5, 6] The insect damages plants by sucking sap and excreting a substance called honeydew, which can lead to sooty mold growth, plant stress, wilting, and in severe cases, death. [3, 6, 8] The pest has since been detected in other Tennessee counties, including Wilson and Sumner. [8, 11] In response, the state is conducting surveillance, outreach, and has deployed specially trained dogs to detect the insect and its egg masses to protect the state's vulnerable wood product and fruit-growing industries. [3, 11] <3> The California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) established a quarantine for the Oriental fruit fly (OFF) in parts of Santa Clara and Contra Costa counties. The action followed the detection of the invasive pest in both areas. [1] A separate quarantine was instituted in East Contra Costa County after several of the invasive flies were found there. [2] <4> A landmark United Nations-backed report from the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) revealed that invasive alien species cost the global economy at least $423 billion annually as of 2019, with these costs having quadrupled every decade since 1970. These invasive species are a major factor in 60% of global plant and animal extinctions and pose significant threats to human well-being and food security by damaging ecosystems, fisheries, and agriculture. The report highlights that impacts are felt globally, with 75% of negative effects occurring in terrestrial environments, particularly forests and cultivated areas. Specific examples of widespread invaders include the water hyacinth, which chokes fisheries. The authors stress that the economic toll is likely a conservative estimate and is projected to continue soaring. <5> The New York State Invasive Species Expo took place from September 24-26, 2023, at Saratoga Spa State Park in Saratoga Springs, NY. The event, sponsored by the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation Invasive Species Coordination Section and statewide partners, was a hands-on conference focused on managing invasive species. For the first time, the expo was open to the public at no cost for general attendance. The theme of the expo was 'Reflect, Adapt, Evolve,' with the goal of reflecting on past accomplishments, learning about new adaptations, and discussing future strategies for confronting the challenges of invasive species. The three-day event featured a variety of activities, including unique presentations, interactive demonstrations, hands-on workshops, small-group discussions, and field trips. A press conference was held on Monday, September 25, to highlight the threat of invasive species. <6> The elm zigzag sawfly (Aproceros leucopoda), an invasive insect native to East Asia, is expanding its range in North America after its initial detection on the continent in Québec, Canada, in 2020. [4, 7, 12, 25] The first confirmed sighting in the United States occurred in Virginia in May 2021. [5, 6, 32] Since then, the pest has been confirmed in several other eastern states, including North Carolina, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York in 2022 [4, 5, 31], followed by Ohio, Massachusetts, and Vermont in 2023. [4, 6, 13] [6, 11] The larvae feed exclusively on elm (Ulmus species) leaves, creating a distinctive zigzag pattern that can lead to significant and even complete defoliation of trees. [23, 25, 29] While this feeding can cause aesthetic damage, weaken trees, and potentially lead to branch dieback from repeated infestations, the long-term impact is still being studied, and there are no definitive reports of the sawfly directly causing tree mortality. [13, 25, 29] <7> Michigan's Governor, Gretchen Whitmer, officially proclaimed July 2023 as Aquatic Invasive Species Awareness Month. This initiative, aimed at protecting the Great Lakes and the state's inland waters, included a specific proclamation for Aquatic Invasive Species Awareness Week from July 2–8, 2023. The stated purpose of the awareness campaign is to encourage behavior change and highlight the importance of preventing the introduction and spread of invasive species that threaten Michigan's aquatic ecosystems. <8> The 'Stop the Spread of Invasive Mussels Act of 2023' (S.2105) was introduced in the U.S. Senate on June 22, 2023, by Senators Michael Bennet and Steve Daines. The proposed legislation authorizes the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Agriculture to take measures to control the movement of aquatic invasive species, such as zebra and quagga mussels, across federal lands and waters. It specifically empowers agencies like the Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, and Forest Service to conduct inspections and decontaminate watercraft. The bill also establishes a grant program, managed by the Bureau of Reclamation, to provide financial assistance to states for establishing, operating, and maintaining watercraft inspection and decontamination stations. <9> In a study published in Nature Communications on June 5, 2023, researchers from the University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture, the University of Massachusetts-Boston, and Washington State University warned that the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal) could severely impact amphibian biodiversity if introduced to North America. [4, 5, 6] Lead author Matt Gray, a professor at the UT School of Natural Resources, stated, “We could see over 80 species of salamanders in the United States and 140 species in North America experience population declines if Bsal is introduced.” [4, 5] The research, which began in 2016, identifies the Appalachian Mountains and the Pacific Northwest as the areas of greatest potential decline due to favorable climates for the pathogen and high salamander populations. [5] The Bsal pathogen, which erodes and destroys amphibian skin, was first discovered in European fire salamander populations a decade prior and has not yet been detected in the Western Hemisphere. [5]

[3, 9] <2> A study published in the journal BioScience highlights the significant role of the horticultural trade in the United States in spreading invasive plant species. Research conducted by the University of Massachusetts Amherst, detailed in a pair of papers, reveals how garden centers contribute to current and future invasions, especially as climate change alters plant-habitable zones. [3] The study, which analyzed 89 invasive plant species across 672 nurseries, discovered that for 55% of these species, they were sold within 13 miles (21 kilometers) of an existing invasion. [3] Projections indicate that if unchecked, the nursery industry could facilitate the spread of 25 invasive species into newly suitable areas with a 2°C increase in warming. [3] The researchers emphasize that their work provides detailed maps and watchlists to identify worrisome species both now and in the coming decades. [3] <3> In an announcement on October 2, 2023, Michigan's Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) confirmed the state's first-ever detection of Hydrilla (Hydrilla verticillata), a highly invasive aquatic plant often considered one of the world's worst. [6, 9] The plant was discovered in September 2023 in two small, adjacent private ponds on residential properties near Berrien Springs in Berrien County. [3] The discovery was made during routine monitoring for another prohibited invasive plant, parrot feather, which had been identified in the ponds in 2020. [6, 7] Michigan State University Extension assisted EGLE in confirming the identification of the hydrilla. [11] In response, EGLE initiated surveys of connected waterways, including the St. Joseph River, and began herbicide treatments to prevent the plant's spread, with a long-term goal of eradication. [5, 6] <4> The Tennessee Department of Agriculture (TDA) officially confirmed the first detection of the invasive spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) in Davidson County on September 28, 2023, making Tennessee the 16th state to identify the pest since its initial U.S. discovery in Pennsylvania in 2014. [3, 5, 7] The confirmation followed a report from a citizen who spotted the insect. [5] This non-native species, originally from Asia, poses a significant threat to various agricultural and natural resources, showing a preference for grapevines, fruit trees, and the invasive Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima). [3, 6, 10] It also affects other trees like maple, black walnut, and yellow-poplar. [5, 6] The insect damages plants by sucking sap and excreting a substance called honeydew, which can lead to sooty mold growth, plant stress, wilting, and in severe cases, death. [3, 6, 8] The pest has since been detected in other Tennessee counties, including Wilson and Sumner. [8, 11] In response, the state is conducting surveillance, outreach, and has deployed specially trained dogs to detect the insect and its egg masses to protect the state's vulnerable wood product and fruit-growing industries. [3, 11] <5> The California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) established a quarantine for the Oriental fruit fly (OFF) in parts of Santa Clara and Contra Costa counties. The action followed the detection of the invasive pest in both areas. In Santa Clara County, a 112-square-mile quarantine was enacted after eight flies were discovered in the cities of Santa Clara and Sunnyvale. [1] A separate quarantine was instituted in East Contra Costa County after several of the invasive flies were found there. [2] <6> A landmark United Nations-backed report from the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) revealed that invasive alien species cost the global economy at least $423 billion annually as of 2019, with these costs having quadrupled every decade since 1970. The report, developed over four years by 86 experts from 49 countries, is considered the most comprehensive assessment on the subject to date. It identifies human activities, such as global trade and travel, as the primary drivers for the spread of over 37,000 alien species, of which at least 3,500 are documented as harmful and invasive. These invasive species are a major factor in 60% of global plant and animal extinctions and pose significant threats to human well-being and food security by damaging ecosystems, fisheries, and agriculture. The report highlights that impacts are felt globally, with 75% of negative effects occurring in terrestrial environments, particularly forests and cultivated areas. Specific examples of widespread invaders include the water hyacinth, which chokes fisheries. The authors stress that the economic toll is likely a conservative estimate and is projected to continue soaring. <7> The New York State Invasive Species Expo took place from September 24-26, 2023, at Saratoga Spa State Park in Saratoga Springs, NY. The event, sponsored by the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation Invasive Species Coordination Section and statewide partners, was a hands-on conference focused on managing invasive species. For the first time, the expo was open to the public at no cost for general attendance. The theme of the expo was 'Reflect, Adapt, Evolve,' with the goal of reflecting on past accomplishments, learning about new adaptations, and discussing future strategies for confronting the challenges of invasive species. The three-day event featured a variety of activities, including unique presentations, interactive demonstrations, hands-on workshops, small-group discussions, and field trips. A press conference was held on Monday, September 25, to highlight the threat of invasive species. <8> The elm zigzag sawfly (Aproceros leucopoda), an invasive insect native to East Asia, is expanding its range in North America after its initial detection on the continent in Québec, Canada, in 2020. [4, 7, 12, 25] The first confirmed sighting in the United States occurred in Virginia in May 2021. [5, 6, 32] Since then, the pest has been confirmed in several other eastern states, including North Carolina, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York in 2022 [4, 5, 31], followed by Ohio, Massachusetts, and Vermont in 2023. [4, 6, 13] [6, 11] The larvae feed exclusively on elm (Ulmus species) leaves, creating a distinctive zigzag pattern that can lead to significant and even complete defoliation of trees. [23, 25, 29] While this feeding can cause aesthetic damage, weaken trees, and potentially lead to branch dieback from repeated infestations, the long-term impact is still being studied, and there are no definitive reports of the sawfly directly causing tree mortality.
